newsitem.title: UK: British banking megamerger would face brick wall.
newsitem.headline: British banking megamerger would face brick wall.

text.p: A rumoured merger between British banking giants Barclays and National Westminster Bank would face insurmountable regulatory hurdles, analysts said on Monday, even though one said it would make "fantastic commercial sense".

The merger, which at current market prices would create a bank with a market value of over 30 billion pounds ($50 billion), could lead to big cost savings but would give the merged group about half Britain's small and medium corporate business, a share likely to ring alarm bells at the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC).

Neither bank would comment on the record other than to say that they never comment on market speculation but sources close to NatWest said the bank had received no approaches from potential merger partners.
Rumours about NatWest have been flying thick and fast since it emerged that it had approached Abbey National recently to discuss a possible merger. Abbey National rebuffed the approach.

The Abbey move by NatWest has been seen as an attempt to shift its strategy away from the recent emphasis on troubled investment banking unit NatWest Markets which last week saw the resignation of its Chief Executive Martin Owen after the unit's poor performance prompted a profits warning.
"I think a merger would make fantastic commercial sense," said David Poutney, banking analyst at Panmure Gordon, "but there are two big problems."

Poutney said these were the competition element and the fact that, to achieve the possible cost savings, which he put at least 600 million pounds per year, there would have to be large scale redundancies which the new Labour Government might frown upon.

The problem such a merger could present is that it would leave the small and medium corporate market sectors without effective competition. To be competitive in these areas, banks need to have a long-term presence in the market and an effective branch network.

In other sectors, such as current accounts and credit cards, a combined Barclays/NatWest giant would also enjoy a big market share -- 38 percent in current accounts -- but would face strong competition from current and emerging players.

Figures from Barclays and NatWest show that a merged bank would have a market share of 55 percent in the medium-sized corporate sector and 48 percent in the small business sector. Both figures are well above the 25 percent figure usually seen as triggering MMC interest.

Salomon Brothers banking analyst John Leonard agreed that the practical barriers would be too great to pull off such a merger which would also face the problem of joining together what he called "duplicative" investment banks in NatWest Markets and the Barclays unit BZW.

The swirl of the Barclays/NatWest rumours reminded some in the City of the attempt by Lloyds Bank to take over Midland Bank in 1992. This foundered for competition reasons although the Lloyds/Midland combination would have had a smaller market share than Barclays/NatWest.

In 1992, HSBC, unencumbered by monopolies considerations, jumped in and bought Midland and some analysts say that a possible foreign buyer could be the best partner for NatWest, even though this would provoke the usual round of xenophobic talk about Britain's financial industry being taken over by foreign predators.
Among names that have been mentioned in this context are Citibank, the commercial banking operation of Citicorp and ABN AMRO, the Dutch banking giant which already owns broker Hoare Govett in London.

A spokeswoman for Citibank declined to comment on the market speculation but banking sources said it is no longer part of the bank's strategy to develop in the UK retail market with the focus firmly on other international business.

Monday's renewed speculation at least did NatWest's share price no harm. The stock, which has underperformed the market for 10 years, was 32 pence higher at 778.5p in a lower bank sector which included Barclays down 11p at 1152.5p per share.
Analysts said the rumours over NatWest were sure to continue.
"There will be many more rumours," said one analyst, "it's inevitable when NatWest is clearly in trouble."
